props.title: The Cardinal

sections.content: The Cardinal stands as Otto Preminger's ambitious chronicle of Catholic Church politics and personal faith, following Stephen Fermoyle's rise from Boston priest to Cardinal during the turbulent period between WWI and WWII. Like Preminger's other epics including Exodus (1960) and Advise and Consent (1962), it tackles controversial topics head-on - anti-Semitism, racism, Nazi persecution, and forbidden romance. Tom Tryon delivers a complex performance as Fermoyle, whose personal struggles mirror larger societal conflicts. The film's scope rivals religious epics like The Song of Bernadette (1943) and The Nun's Story (1959), but with Preminger's characteristic unflinching examination of institutional power.

sections.content: Preminger's signature long takes and deep focus cinematography create an intimate yet expansive feel, particularly effective in the Vatican sequences. The film's nearly three-hour runtime allows for detailed exploration of Catholic doctrine and church politics while maintaining personal stakes through Fermoyle's family drama. This approach influenced later religious-themed films like The Mission (1986) and The Name of the Rose (1986), which similarly balance institutional commentary with individual moral struggles.

The film's treatment of interfaith marriage and racial prejudice was groundbreaking for 1963, predating similar themes in Guess Who's Coming to Dinner (1967). Particularly powerful are scenes dealing with Fermoyle's sister's interfaith romance and his confrontation with Austrian anti-Semitism. Cinematographer Leon Shamroy's Oscar-nominated work captures both the grandeur of Vatican ceremonies and intimate family moments with equal skill. SUBHEAD: Religious Cinema in Transition

sections.content: The Cardinal marked a shift in Hollywood's portrayal of religious institutions, moving from reverent epics like The Robe (1953) to more nuanced examinations of faith and power. Its influence can be seen in later films like True Confessions (1981) and Mass Appeal (1984), which similarly explore conflicts between personal conscience and institutional authority. The film's willingness to address controversial topics within a religious context paved the way for more critical examinations like Spotlight (2015).
